description: Composite figure on Fe-6.8Al low-density steel mixing two mechanical-property plots with a data table; the caption's panel lettering is inconsistent with the pixels (it calls the table "(a)" and groups the curves under "(b)"). Panel (a): engineering stress-strain curves, y-axis "Engineering Stress (MPa)" 0-2000 (200 MPa gridlines), x-axis "Engineering strain (%)" 0-40 (5% gridlines); legend: black = 98% CR, red = 5 min, blue = 60 min. The black 98% CR curve rises almost vertically to a maximum just under the 1800 MPa line at ~2% strain, then falls steeply and terminates near the 5% gridline around 1250 MPa. The red 5 min curve yields near 700 MPa, flattens to a broad maximum near 860-870 MPa between ~15 and 20% strain, then softens, terminating close to the 30% gridline. The blue 60 min curve is lowest: yield ~300 MPa, plateau ~395 MPa, ending near 38% at ~230 MPa. Table 4 (middle) lists condition vs yield strength (MPa), ultimate tensile strength (MPa), % uniform elongation and yield ratio (YS/UTS): 98%CR 1800, –, 1.2, –; 750 °C 5 min 700, 870, 20.0, 0.85; 750 °C 60 min 265, 394, 29.8, 0.67. Panel (b): "Rate of strain hardening (MPa)" 0-50000 vs "True strain" 0.00-0.20; blue (60 min) lies above red (5 min) at all strains; both spike sharply at very low strain then decay almost monotonically toward zero near 0.20. Together they show that 98% CR gives very high strength but negligible ductility, while annealing softens the steel and raises ductility.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress-strain plot for Fe-6.8Al; y-axis Engineering Stress (MPa) 0-2000, x-axis Engineering strain (%) 0-40. Legend: 98% CR (black), 5 min (red), 60 min (blue). Black peaks just below 1800 MPa at ~2% strain and terminates near 5% strain at ~1250 MPa; red plateaus near 860-870 MPa and ends near the 30% gridline; blue plateaus ~395 MPa and ends near 38% at ~230 MPa.

Data table of sample condition versus yield strength (MPa), ultimate tensile strength (MPa), % uniform elongation and yield ratio (= YS/UTS): 98%CR 1800, –, 1.2, –; 750 °C, 5 min 700, 870, 20.0, 0.85; 750 °C, 60 min 265, 394, 29.8, 0.67.

Rate of strain hardening (MPa, 0-50000) versus true strain (0.00-0.20) for Fe-6.8Al annealed at 750 °C for 5 min (red) and 60 min (blue). Both curves show a steep initial spike followed by a small local maximum near true strain ~0.02 and then a monotonic decay; the blue 60 min curve lies above the red 5 min curve at all strains.

observations.observation: Panel (a) plots engineering stress (MPa, 0-2000) against engineering strain (%, 0-40) with three curves labelled in the legend as 98% CR (black), 5 min (red) and 60 min (blue).
The 98% CR curve in (a) reaches its maximum just below the 1800 MPa gridline at roughly 2% strain, then drops steeply and terminates near the 5% strain gridline at about 1250 MPa.
The 5 min curve in (a) yields at about 700 MPa, forms a broad plateau at ~860-870 MPa between ~15 and 20% strain, and terminates close to the 30% strain gridline.
The 60 min curve in (a) is the lowest-strength one, with a plateau at ~395 MPa extending to about 38% strain before falling to ~230 MPa.

The table lists sample conditions 98%CR (YS 1800 MPa, UTS '-', uniform elongation 1.2%, yield ratio '-'), 750 °C 5 min (700 MPa, 870 MPa, 20.0%, 0.85) and 750 °C 60 min (265 MPa, 394 MPa, 29.8%, 0.67).

The visible red (5 min) curve in (a) extends to near the 30% strain gridline, whereas the accompanying table lists only 20.0% uniform elongation for that condition - an apparent pixel/caption-table mismatch reported with low confidence.
Panel (b) plots the rate of strain hardening (MPa, 0-50000) against true strain (0.00-0.20) for the 5 min (red) and 60 min (blue) annealed samples.
In (b) the blue 60 min curve lies above the red 5 min curve over the entire true-strain range, and the blue initial rise exceeds the 50000 MPa upper axis limit (off-scale).
In (b) both curves show a rapid initial drop followed by a small local maximum near true strain ~0.02 and then a gradual, near-monotonic decay toward zero at true strain ~0.20.
The citing text states that the yield strength of the 98% CR sample (= 1800 MPa) is much higher than that of the sample annealed at 750 °C for 60 min (= 265 MPa).

The citing text attributes the strength difference to dislocation density changing from ~2.2 x 10^15 m^-2 (98% CR) to ~10^12 m^-2 (annealed 750 °C, 60 min), identifying dislocation strengthening as a main mechanism.

The citing text states the yield ratio of the fully annealed sample (750 °C, 60 min) is lower than that of the 98%CR sample, and that the higher hardening rate occurs in the sample annealed for 60 min rather than 5 min.
